analysis.one_liner: Freezes most class action lawsuits over illegal mortgage kickbacks through 1998.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote; it sat in two House subcommittees and died when the 105th Congress ended, despite 133 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have placed a moratorium, lasting from enactment through December 31, 1998, on class action lawsuits filed under the Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act (RESPA) [S2]. RESPA is the federal law that prohibits lenders and mortgage brokers from taking undisclosed kickbacks in home-sale transactions. The bill would have stopped courts from certifying consumer classes, halted discovery on class issues, and froze cases already certified after January 1, 1996 — except where a class was certified to approve a settlement [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Mortgage lenders and mortgage brokers facing class actions alleging illegal kickbacks would benefit most: the bill would pause nearly all such cases, block the class certification that gives suits their leverage, and shield parties from sanctions for not cooperating with discovery [S3]. Homebuyers, who use these class actions as their main tool to recover overcharges from hidden referral fees, would lose that remedy for the duration of the moratorium.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Mortgage lenders and brokers facing kickback suits

how_it_helps.text: Bars courts from certifying any class in RESPA kickback cases, except to approve a settlement, removing the leverage that class actions give homebuyers over lenders [S3].
Stays all proceedings in cases where a class was certified on or after January 1, 1996, freezing suits already underway through the end of 1998 [S3].
Prohibits discovery into class certification issues and blocks sanctions for refusing to comply, reducing litigation costs and pressure on lenders to settle [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Homebuyers and borrowers who allege they paid inflated settlement charges because of undisclosed referral fees between lenders and mortgage brokers would lose, at least temporarily, their most effective enforcement mechanism — the class action [S3]. Consumer plaintiffs with cases already certified would see them frozen, and the statute of limitations would keep running.

drawbacks.text: Supporters argued that RESPA class actions were being used to extract costly settlements from lenders over technical kickback allegations, with costs passed on to borrowers; the bill preserved only settlement-driven certifications, allowing cases to resolve by agreement while blocking litigation-driven ones [S3].
The moratorium was indiscriminate: it would freeze meritorious cases along with weak ones, and while cases were stayed, the clock on borrowers' legal deadlines kept running, eroding claims [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered lenders relief from a wave of kickback litigation, but its cost fell on the very consumers the underlying law protects: for the length of the moratorium, homebuyers would have had almost no practical way to pursue collectively the undisclosed referral fees RESPA bans. Because it froze existing cases and blocked new certifications without any alternative remedy for consumers, the burden fell squarely on ordinary borrowers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Banking and Judiciary committees and their subcommittees, never got a hearing or a floor vote, and expired when the Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 10, 1997, by Rep. Robert Ehrlich with 18 original cosponsors, and referred to both the Banking and Financial Services Committee and the Judiciary Committee [S5].

On April 15 it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Courts and Intellectual Property, and on April 25 to the Banking Subcommittee on Housing and Community Opportunity; no further action was ever taken [S5].
The bill attracted 133 cosponsors — 104 Republicans and 29 Democrats — but was never scheduled for a committee markup or a vote in either chamber [S4].
The 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, and the bill died without any vote having been taken on it [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Homebuyers and consumer plaintiffs came out ahead: the class action tool they use against hidden mortgage kickbacks remained fully available. Lenders and mortgage brokers did not get the two-year litigation freeze they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Homebuyers kept their right to sue

for.name: Rep. Robert L. Ehrlich Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to impose a moratorium on RESPA class action lawsuits

against.name: House Banking and Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee on April 25, 1997, and took no further action; no markup or vote was ever scheduled

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee on April 15, 1997, and took no further action

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was broad but skewed heavily Republican: 104 of 227 House Republicans signed on versus 29 of 208 House Democrats.

industries.note: The bill would have given the industry a two-year shield from class actions alleging illegal referral-fee kickbacks under RESPA, halting certification of consumer classes and freezing cases already certified. Its gain would come directly at the cost of homebuyers' remedy for overcharges.
RESPA kickback class actions were a growing area of consumer practice; a certification moratorium and a discovery freeze would have dried up that work for the moratorium period.
